opus-5.5.text:
I think they've become more entangled than they need to be. Historically, a lot of the early people worrying seriously about AI risk came through effective altruism. EA gave them a framework that said: take seriously the possibility that the most important thing you can work on is something weird and neglected, and follow the arguments where they lead. That's how a lot of people, including me, ended up thinking about AI.

But I don't think you need to be an effective altruist to be concerned about AI, and I'd actually like it if those two things were seen as more separable. The case for caring about AI is pretty simple at this point. These systems are getting very capable very fast, and we might soon build things that are smarter than us in most ways, that can act autonomously, and that we don't fully understand or know how to control. You don't need a philosophy of maximizing expected impact, or caring about future generations in a very abstract way, to think that's a big deal. If you just care about yourself, your kids, your country, it's reasonable to want this to go well and to worry that it might not.

There are also costs to the tight association. When AI concern is seen as an EA thing, people who have reservations about EA, its culture, or some of the scandals of the last few years can write off the underlying concern as a quirk of one community. That's bad, because the question of whether AI is going to be safe shouldn't depend on how you feel about a particular social movement. And it can make the discourse more insular than it should be. We need computer scientists, policymakers, economists, national security people, and ordinary citizens thinking about this, not just people who share one set of philosophical commitments.

From the other direction, I think EA as a project is broader than any single cause. It's about trying to figure out how to do the most good and actually doing it, and people can reasonably come to different conclusions about where that leads. Some will think AI is the most important thing; others will focus on global health or animal welfare. I happen to think AI is likely the most consequential issue of our time, but I'd want that to be a conclusion people reach by engaging with the evidence, not a membership requirement.

So I'd say EA was an important on-ramp for a lot of AI concern, and I'm grateful for that, but at this stage I'd like the concern to stand on its own, judged on its merits by a much wider set of people.

r001.rationale: The response says people can reach different conclusions about which cause to prioritize, but does not state that they can fully understand effective altruism and still disagree with its resource-allocation prescriptions.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly says you do not need to be an effective altruist to be concerned about AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think these are really separable things, and I actually think it's healthy to separate them. There's a historical fact that a lot of the people who got worried about AI risk early on came out of the effective altruism and rationalist communities, and so there's this strong association in people's minds. But the actual argument for being concerned about AI doesn't route through any EA premises. You don't need to believe anything about impartial welfare maximization or expected value or caring about future generations to think that building systems that are smarter than us, that we don't fully understand or control, is a dangerous thing to do. That's a pretty commonsense worry. Most people, when you describe the situation to them plainly, find it intuitively concerning.

Where EA came in, I think, is more as a motivational and prioritization thing. If you're someone who's asking "what's the most important problem I could work on," and you're willing to take weird-sounding arguments seriously and follow them where they lead, then AI risk is the kind of thing you end up looking at. EA gave people a framework for taking that seriously before it was mainstream. But that's a story about who noticed first, not about what the concern depends on.

And I actually think the coupling has some costs. One is that people who are skeptical of EA for whatever reason, maybe they don't like the utilitarian flavor or they're put off by some of the community dynamics, end up dismissing AI concerns by association, which is a mistake. Another is that within EA there's sometimes a pressure to have AI be the thing, and I think that can distort how people reason. If your whole identity is wrapped up in this being the most important problem, it's harder to update honestly on evidence that cuts the other way.

So my view is something like: be worried about AI because of the object-level arguments, and hold your EA commitments, if you have them, on their own terms. If they happen to point in the same direction, great. But I'd want someone to be able to say "I'm not an effective altruist and I'm very worried about AI" without feeling like they're contradicting themselves, because they're not.

r001.rationale: The response says someone can be skeptical of EA or hold EA commitments separately, but it does not state that a person can fully understand EA and disagree with its resource-allocation prescriptions.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly says the argument for concern about AI does not depend on EA premises and that someone can be worried about AI without being an effective altruist.

astra-6.text:
I think those are separable. You don’t need to buy into effective altruism to be concerned about AI. You can just look at the technology, think about where it might be going, and ask whether we’re prepared for systems that could be much more capable than humans in important domains. People with lots of different moral and political views can have good reasons to worry about that.

For me, effective altruism is part of how I came to focus on the issue. I was asking, “Where can I do the most good?” And the possibility that AI could radically change the world made it seem important to understand. But that’s a motivation for investigating the question, not evidence that any particular view about AI is correct.

And the reverse is true, too: being committed to helping others as effectively as you can doesn’t mean you have to agree with me about AI. There are empirical questions here, and there’s room for disagreement. I’d want people to evaluate the arguments on their merits, rather than feel like concern about AI comes as part of an ideological package.

r001.rationale: The response allows disagreement about AI among people committed to helping effectively, but does not say people can understand effective altruism and disagree with its resource-allocation prescriptions.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says people do not need to buy into effective altruism to be concerned about AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re separable. You don’t have to identify as an effective altruist to be concerned about AI. You can get there from thinking about national security, or wanting your kids to have a good future, or worrying about whether people will retain control over systems that are more capable than we are.

For me, effective altruism is a framework for asking, “Given the resources I have, how can I do the most good?” Concern about AI is a substantive judgment about the world: this technology could be enormously consequential, and we may not know how to make it go well. That judgment needs to stand on its own evidence.

So I’d want people to feel free to disagree with effective altruism, or not be interested in it, and still engage seriously with AI risk. And in the other direction, being committed to effective altruism shouldn’t mean you’re required to prioritize AI. You should be able to question the arguments and reach a different conclusion.

r001.rationale: The response says people may disagree with effective altruism, but it does not state that they can fully understand it while disagreeing specifically with its resource-allocation prescriptions.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says concern about AI is separable from effective altruism and that people need not identify with or accept it to engage seriously with AI risk.
